source.title: $100M Offers
source.author: Alex Hormozi
source.note: The exercises and ideas below are the book's, said in this tool's own words. Read the book for the reasoning and the stories; use this to do the work in order and keep what you wrote.

bands.name: Sketch
bands.meaning: Where you stand today, in rough strokes

bands.name: Build
bands.meaning: The book's exercise for this part, done properly

bands.name: Sharpen
bands.meaning: Score it, check it against the book, tighten it

bands.name: Prove
bands.meaning: Take it in front of real people

rings.title: Your offer in one line
rings.says: Every planet has a sketch. The Sky can say your offer in one sentence, and the offer sheet opens with its first lines.

rings.title: The Grand Slam draft
rings.says: The market is chosen, the problems have solutions, the stack has a price, the enhancers are written. The offer sheet is a full draft.

rings.title: Scored and checked
rings.says: The value equation is rated before and after, every checklist is ticked, every piece has a name and a price.

rings.title: Launched
rings.says: It went in front of real prospects. The Sky shows what they said and what it closed.

planets.label: Crowd
planets.what: The book starts with who, not what. A commodity is anything a buyer compares on price alone; the way out is to be the only one who does what you do, for a crowd that badly wants it. A good market shows four signs: massive pain, purchasing power, easy to target, and growing. The three big markets are health, wealth and relationships, and the money is in a narrow slice of one of them. Pick the slice and stay.

planets.label: Price
planets.what: Lowering a price starts a vicious cycle: less margin, less service, worse results, less proof, so more pressure to lower it again. Raising it starts the opposite cycle: clients who pay more are more invested and get better results, and the margin funds better delivery. The book's rule is to charge so much it hurts, then build so much value that the price feels small.

planets.label: Value
planets.what: Value is what the buyer feels, and it has four parts. On top: the dream outcome (how much they want it) times the perceived likelihood that it will work for them. Underneath: the time delay before they see it, times the effort and sacrifice it asks of them. Raise the top, shrink the bottom. The bottom matters most, and the book's goal for it is zero.

planets.label: Offer
planets.what: First loosen up (divergent thinking, the brick exercise). Then list every problem the client will hit on the way to the dream outcome, turn each one into a solution, brainstorm ways to deliver every solution, and sort those by value and cost. Keep what is high value; drop what is low value and high cost. What is left, named and priced, is the stack.

planets.label: Enhancers
planets.what: Four things make a good offer irresistible without changing the core. Scarcity: a real limit on how many can have it. Urgency: a real reason to decide now. Bonuses: named extras, each solving one specific worry, priced and justified, ideally tools rather than more training. Guarantees: unconditional, conditional, anti, or implied, and they can be stacked. All four must be true.

planets.label: Name
planets.chapters: Section IV, chapter 15, and Section V
planets.what: A name is the wrapper, and a wrapper can be refreshed without touching the offer. The book's formula is MAGIC: a Magnetic reason why, Announce the avatar, Give them a goal, Indicate a time interval, Complete with a container word. When an offer tires, change the name, the bonuses, the guarantee or the urgency, not the core.

terms.says: An offer so good people feel silly saying no: a big promise, made believable, delivered fast and with little effort, with a price far below what it is worth to them.
Something buyers compare on price because every seller's version looks the same.
A market with massive pain, money to spend, a place you can reach it, and more people arriving each year.
Dream outcome times perceived likelihood, over time delay times effort and sacrifice.
The result the client pictures, said as status and feeling, not as your process.
How sure the client feels that this will work for them, given who they are.
How long between paying and noticing the result. Fast wins shrink it.
What the client has to do and give up to get the result. Done for you shrinks it.
The ways one solution can be delivered: group size, how much you do for them, the medium, the speed.
Sort every delivery idea by value to the client and cost to you; keep the high value ones, drop the rest, then bundle what is left.
A true limit on supply: seats, clients per month, a bonus for the first few.
A true reason the decision cannot wait: a start date, a season, a deadline, a closing window.
A named extra added after the core offer and its price, each one answering a specific worry.
What happens if it does not work: unconditional, conditional, anti (all sales final, with a reason), or implied (you pay by result).
Magnetic reason why, Announce the avatar, Give them a goal, Indicate a time interval, Complete with a container word.
The name, bonuses, guarantee and urgency around the core. Refresh the wrapper when an offer tires; keep the core.

levels.title: What you sell today
levels.prompt: In one sentence, what do you sell, and to whom?
levels.help: Say it the way you would to a stranger. The second question is the book's commodity test: if buyers pick on price, the offer is a commodity, and the rest of these planets is how to stop being one.

fields.label: What you sell, and to whom
When a prospect compares you with others, what do they decide on?

options.label: Mostly price, with a bit of trust.
Mostly what they get, price second.
Something only I offer. Price barely comes up.

payoff.say: Where you sit between commodity and category of one.

levels.checkpoint: You can say what you sell in one breath and you know whether price is the deciding factor.

levels.title: The market you are in
levels.prompt: Which of the three big markets is this, and who buys from you now?
levels.help: The book names health, wealth and relationships as the three markets that never go away. Most offers live inside one of them. Who buys now is your starting avatar; you will narrow it in band 3.

fields.label: Who buys from you now, in a few words

payoff.say: Your starting avatar, named.

levels.checkpoint: The big market is chosen and the current buyer is named.

levels.title: The four signs of a starving crowd
levels.prompt: Score this crowd on the book's four signs, 1 to 5 each.
levels.help: Massive pain: they need it, not just want it. Purchasing power: they can pay. Easy to target: there is a place, list or group where they gather. Growing: more of them every year. The book says a great offer in a bad market still starves.

fields.label: Massive pain
fields.hint: 1 is a mild wish, 5 is a problem that keeps them up at night

fields.label: Purchasing power
fields.hint: 1 is no spare money, 5 is they already spend on this

fields.label: Easy to target
fields.hint: 1 is scattered everywhere, 5 is one group or list holds them

payoff.say: The four bars, the total out of 20, and the weakest sign.

levels.checkpoint: All four signs are scored and you can name the weakest.

levels.title: The pain in their words
levels.prompt: Write three things this crowd says or complains about, in their own words.
levels.help: Not your words for it, theirs. Messages, reviews, what they said on a call. These lines come back on the Offer planet, where every problem becomes a solution, and on the Name planet.

payoff.say: Their words, kept for the problems list.

levels.checkpoint: Three real lines, none of them written by you.

levels.title: The niche ladder
levels.prompt: Start broad, then narrow three times. At each rung, write the price the same help could sell for.
levels.help: The book's example goes from time management for anyone, to time management for salespeople, to salespeople in one industry, with the price rising many times over at each step, for nearly the same content. Try it with yours. Broad at the top, narrowest at the bottom.

payoff.say: Price against specificity, rung by rung.

levels.checkpoint: At least three rungs, each narrower than the last, each with a price.

levels.title: Commit to one
levels.prompt: Pick the rung you will serve, and tick what makes it safe to commit.
levels.help: The book's warning is that people switch niches before the niche can pay them. Pick one rung and give it long enough to learn its language. This is the avatar every later planet reads.

fields.label: The niche you commit to, in a few words

items.label: I can name where these people gather: a place, a group, a list
They can pay what I plan to charge
There are more of them each year, or at least not fewer
I will stay with this niche long enough to learn its language

payoff.say: Your avatar, the person every other planet is built for.

levels.checkpoint: One niche named and all four boxes ticked.

levels.title: Where to find them
levels.prompt: List the places you can reach this crowd, and roughly how many are in each.
levels.help: A group, a list, a channel, an event, a partner who already serves them. A rough count is fine; it tells you whether the crowd is big enough to feed the price.

payoff.say: Your reach, added up.

levels.checkpoint: Two or more places with a rough count each.

levels.title: Prove the crowd is starving
levels.prompt: Do these in the world, then tick them.
levels.help: A crowd is proven by what people do and say, not by what you believe. Each line is one conversation or one search.

items.label: Talked to three people in the niche about the pain
Found one paid alternative they already spend money on
Found one sign the market is growing: a trend, a count, a new rule
Wrote down the exact words they use for the problem (band 2)

payoff.say: The crowd is proven, and the four signs are backed by something real.

levels.checkpoint: All four ticked.

levels.title: Your price today
levels.chapter: Chapter 5, charge what it is worth
levels.prompt: What do you charge now, and what does one delivery cost you?
levels.help: Cost is your time at the rate you would pay someone else, plus materials, tools and the refunds you eat. A rough figure is fine. The reveal is your margin, the number the vicious cycle eats first.

fields.label: What one delivery costs you, roughly

payoff.say: Your gross margin today.

levels.checkpoint: Price, how it is charged, and a rough cost are all in.

levels.title: Where you sit
levels.prompt: Against the alternatives your crowd sees, where does your price sit, and how often does a pitch close?
levels.help: Be honest about the position; the book's whole argument is that the top of the range is the safest place to stand. The close rate is your baseline for the Prove band.

fields.label: Of ten people you pitch, how many say yes, as a percent

payoff.say: Your position and your close rate, kept for the before and after.

levels.checkpoint: A position and a close rate.

levels.title: Which cycle you are in
levels.chapter: Chapter 5, the vicious and virtuous cycles
levels.prompt: Tick every line that is true of your business this year.
levels.help: The book draws two loops. Lowering price cuts margin, which cuts service, which cuts results, which cuts proof, which pushes price lower. Raising price does the opposite at every step. Tick honestly; the picture shows which loop you are riding.

options.label: I lower the price to win deals
Clients expect a lot and value it little
I cannot afford to give the service I would like to
Clients get worse results than they could
I am always chasing the next sale
I resent some of the work
The clients who pay more are the most committed
The clients who pay more get better results
The margin pays for better help and better marketing
I am proud to say the price
Good clients send more good clients

payoff.say: Which loop you are in, drawn.

levels.checkpoint: Both lists looked at; the picture names your loop.

levels.title: What the outcome is worth
levels.prompt: If the client gets the dream outcome, what is it worth to them in money over a year? Defend the number.
levels.help: Revenue they gain, cost they stop paying, time they get back at their rate, a price they would pay to make a pain stop. The gap between this number and your price is what makes an offer a Grand Slam.

fields.label: Worth to the client, a year

payoff.say: Worth against price: the gap, as a multiple.

levels.checkpoint: A number and the sentence that defends it.

levels.title: Charge so much it hurts
levels.prompt: Pick a price that makes you a little uncomfortable to say out loud, and the revenue you want in a year.
levels.help: The book's test: raise it until it hurts. The picture shows how many clients each price needs to reach your revenue goal, and the margin at each. Fewer clients, more care each, better results, more proof.

fields.label: The new price, charged the same way as today
Revenue you want in a year

payoff.say: Clients needed at the old price and the new one, and the margin at each.

levels.checkpoint: A new price and a yearly goal.

levels.title: The premium price checklist
levels.prompt: Tick each once it is true.
levels.help: These are the conditions the book puts around a high price. If a line is not true yet, the Offer and Enhancers planets are where it gets fixed.

items.label: I can say the new price without apologising or adding a discount
The offer gives back many times the price (the worth to price gap is 3 to 1 or better)
I know what I will add so the price feels small (the Offer planet)
I have stopped comparing my price with the cheapest alternative

payoff.say: The gap at the new price.

levels.checkpoint: All four ticked.

levels.title: Say it out loud
levels.prompt: Offer the new price to three real prospects and write down what each one said.
levels.help: Not a survey. A real pitch, with the new number. Their answers are data, and a no at a high price teaches more than a yes at a low one.

payoff.say: The close rate at the new price, against the old.

levels.checkpoint: Three real answers.

levels.title: Read your margin now
levels.prompt: Here is your margin at the new price, with the delivery cost from your stack where you have one. Does it look right?
levels.help: A confirm level: the app worked it out, you say yes or go back and fix a number. Confirming it counts the level.

payoff.say: Margin at the new price, confirmed.

levels.checkpoint: Confirmed.

levels.title: Rate the offer as it is
levels.prompt: Score your current offer on the four parts of the value equation, 1 to 10 each.
levels.help: Dream outcome: how big and how wanted is the result (10 is life-changing). Perceived likelihood: how sure they feel it will work for them (10 is certain). Time delay: how long until they notice a result (10 is a very long wait). Effort and sacrifice: how much they must do and give up (10 is a great deal). The score is top over bottom.

fields.label: Effort and sacrifice (10 is a lot)

payoff.say: The equation, drawn, with your score.

levels.checkpoint: Four scores and a first value score.

levels.title: The dream outcome
levels.prompt: Write the result they want, in their words. Not what you do; what they get, and who they get to be.
levels.help: The book separates the outcome from the process. Nobody wants a workout plan; they want to be the parent who keeps up. Status and feeling count more than features.

fields.label: The dream outcome, in their words
Who they get to be, in the eyes of people they care about

payoff.say: The top of the equation, written down. Every other planet reads it.

levels.checkpoint: An outcome and a status line.

levels.title: Why they will believe it
levels.prompt: List the proof that makes a stranger believe this will work for someone like them.
levels.help: Results you got yourself, results clients got, credentials, a guarantee, a sample they can try, plain numbers. The more it looks like them, the more it counts.

payoff.say: Your proof, by kind.

levels.checkpoint: Two or more pieces of proof, at least one about a client.

levels.title: Time to the first win
levels.prompt: What is the first thing they will notice, how soon, and how long to the full result?
levels.help: The book's fix for a long time delay is a fast win: something real inside days, while the big result takes its time. Say both plainly and the wait stops feeling like a gamble.

payoff.say: The first win and the full result on one line.

levels.checkpoint: A first win with a day count, and the weeks to the full result.

levels.title: What it costs them beyond money
levels.prompt: Every hour, habit and thing they must give up. Then how the offer takes each one off them.
levels.help: Sacrifice is the part of the equation buyers feel most and sellers forget. If a line has no fix yet, write the fix you would build if you had to.

cols.label: What they must do or give up
How the offer removes or softens it

payoff.say: How many sacrifices have a fix.

levels.checkpoint: Three or more, every one with a fix.

levels.title: Tighten the bottom of the equation
levels.prompt: Tick each once the offer does it.
levels.help: The book's aim for the bottom of the equation is zero: no wait, no work. You will not reach zero; each tick moves you toward it.

items.label: Promises a first win inside the first week, or says exactly when
Asks the client to learn nothing they do not already use
Does the hardest step with them or for them
Has a fix for every sacrifice on the list

payoff.say: How tight the bottom of the equation is.

levels.checkpoint: All four ticked.

levels.title: Rate the new offer
levels.prompt: Score the offer again, as it stands after the Offer and Enhancers planets.
levels.help: Same four scales as band 1. Be as hard on it as a stranger would be. The picture puts the two scores side by side.

fields.label: Effort and sacrifice (10 is a lot)

payoff.say: Before and after, on the same scale.

levels.checkpoint: Four new scores.

levels.title: Read the change
levels.prompt: Here is how the value score moved. Does it look right?
levels.help: If the score barely moved, the bottom of the equation is where to look: time delay and effort are where most offers are still heavy.

payoff.say: The change, confirmed.

levels.checkpoint: Confirmed.

levels.title: Warm up: the brick
levels.prompt: Start the two minute timer and list every use you can think of for a brick.
levels.help: The book uses this to switch on divergent thinking before the offer work: many answers, no judging. A doorstop, a weight, a bookend, a step. Quantity is the point.

payoff.say: How many you found, and whether you are warmed up.

levels.checkpoint: Five or more, without stopping to judge them.

levels.title: The trip from here to there
levels.prompt: List the steps your client goes through, from today to the dream outcome, in order.
levels.help: Before the problems come the steps: the book has you walk the client's path and stop at each place something can go wrong. Three to eight steps is typical. The dream outcome comes from the Value planet.

payoff.say: The path, drawn as steps.

levels.checkpoint: Three or more steps, in order.

levels.title: Every problem
levels.prompt: For each step: what goes wrong, what they fear, what takes too long, what is a hassle. Tag each with the part of the value equation it hurts.
levels.help: The book asks for everything, before, during and after. Aim past ten. The tag matters later: problems of time and effort become the delivery pieces; problems of belief become proof and guarantees. Their own words from the Crowd planet belong here.

cols.label: How to (filled in the next level)

payoff.say: Problems by the part of the equation they hurt.

levels.checkpoint: Eight or more problems, each tagged.

levels.title: Every problem becomes a solution
levels.prompt: Turn each problem into a how to line: how to get the outcome even if, or without, the problem. One per row.
levels.help: The book's move is mechanical on purpose: a problem flipped is a solution, and a full list of solutions is the raw material for the stack. Do not judge them yet; the next band trims.

payoff.say: Solutions written against problems.

levels.checkpoint: Every problem has a how to line.

levels.title: Ways to deliver each solution
levels.prompt: For each solution, pick how it could be delivered, then rate its value to the client and its cost to you.
levels.help: The book's delivery questions: one to one, small group or one to many; do it yourself, done with you or done for you; live, recorded, written or a tool; how fast they get help. Two more: if you charged ten times the price, what would you do? If you charged a tenth, what would you have to do? Rate each idea high or low on value and on cost.

payoff.say: The trim and stack grid: keep, keep some, cut.

levels.checkpoint: Five or more ideas, each rated on value and cost.

levels.title: Trim and stack
levels.prompt: High value and low cost stays. High value and high cost stays if you can afford it. Low value goes. Does the sort look right?
levels.help: Confirm the sort or go back and re-rate an idea. What stays is the stack, which the next level names and prices.

payoff.say: The stack, sorted and confirmed.

levels.checkpoint: Confirmed.

levels.title: Name and price every piece
levels.prompt: Give each kept piece a name a client would repeat, say what it solves, and the price it would sell for on its own.
levels.help: The book prices each piece as if sold alone so the stack adds up to a total far above the price. Names should sound like things, not activities: the Launch Checklist, not some checklists. Your cost per piece is optional and feeds the margin read on the Price planet.

payoff.say: The stack's total against your price.

levels.checkpoint: Three or more named, priced pieces.

levels.title: The offer checklist
levels.prompt: Tick each once it is true of the stack.
levels.help: These are the book's conditions for a finished core offer. A line you cannot tick points at the level to go back to.

items.label: Every problem on the list is solved by a piece of the stack or a bonus
Nothing low value and high cost survived the trim
The stack adds up to many times the price
The hardest thing for the client is done for them or with them
Each piece has a name a client would repeat

payoff.say: The stack, checked.

levels.checkpoint: All five ticked.

levels.title: Show it to someone
levels.prompt: Walk two people who fit the niche through the stack. Write what they said and what you changed.
levels.help: Not friends who will be kind. People who could buy. Watch where they lean in and where they glaze over; the stack is not finished until it has been said out loud.

payoff.say: Feedback in, changes made.

levels.checkpoint: Two conversations written down.

levels.title: What you use today
levels.prompt: Which of the four enhancers does your offer already use?
levels.help: Scarcity, urgency, bonuses and a guarantee. Most offers use none of them on purpose. The picture shows the four tiles and which are lit.

options.label: Scarcity: a real limit on how many
Urgency: a real reason to decide now

payoff.say: Four tiles: which are lit.

levels.checkpoint: Answered, even if the answer is none.

levels.title: What holds them back
levels.prompt: List the reasons people give for not buying, in their words.
levels.help: The book pairs every bonus with one specific worry and shapes the guarantee around the biggest one. Write the worries first, so the enhancers have something to answer.

payoff.say: The worries, kept for the bonuses and the guarantee.

levels.checkpoint: Three or more.

levels.title: Scarcity, honestly
levels.prompt: What is the true limit on how many people can have this, and why is it true?
levels.help: The book's kinds: a limited number of clients or seats each period, a bonus only for the first few, a version that will not be sold again. A false limit costs more trust than it earns. Your hours, your capacity and the cohort size are where real limits come from.

options.label: A limited number of clients or seats each period
A bonus only for the first few
This version goes away after the window

payoff.say: Your scarcity, in one line.

levels.checkpoint: A kind, a number where there is one, and the reason.

levels.title: Urgency, honestly
levels.prompt: What is the true reason the decision cannot wait, and by when?
levels.help: The book's kinds: a cohort with a start date, a seasonal or themed promotion, a price or bonus that ends on a date, an opportunity that closes on its own. The date must be one you will hold.

options.label: A cohort with a start date
An opportunity that closes on its own

payoff.say: Your urgency, and the days left.

levels.checkpoint: A kind, a date where there is one, and the reason.

levels.title: Bonuses
levels.prompt: Name three or more bonuses. Each answers one worry, has a price of its own, and something that proves it.
levels.help: The book's rules. Offer them after the core price. Give each a name. Say which worry it answers. Put a price on it and say why. Show proof or paint the picture. Prefer tools, checklists and templates to more training. A partner's product can be a bonus. The worries come from band 1.

options.label: Access to you or a group

cols.label: Proof or the picture it paints

payoff.say: Core stack, bonuses and price on one bar.

levels.checkpoint: Three or more bonuses, each priced and tied to a worry.

levels.title: The bonus checklist
levels.prompt: Tick each once it is true of your bonuses.
levels.help: The book's own list for bonuses, as ticks.

items.label: Each bonus has a name of its own
Each bonus answers one specific worry from the list
Each has a price and one line saying why it is worth that
Each has proof, or a picture of life with it
At least one is a tool, checklist or template rather than more training
They are offered after the core price is named, not folded into it

payoff.say: The bonuses, checked.

levels.checkpoint: All six ticked.

levels.title: The guarantee
levels.prompt: Pick the kind of guarantee and write it in the exact words you will use.
levels.help: Unconditional: money back, no questions. Conditional: do these steps and get this result, or this happens. Anti guarantee: all sales final, with the reason said out loud. Implied: you pay when it works, or by result. The book stacks two where it can, and frames a conditional one as: if you do X, you get Y, or Z.

fields.label: What the client must do for it to hold

payoff.say: Your guarantee as a card.

levels.checkpoint: A kind and the exact words.

levels.title: Enhancers you can stand behind
levels.prompt: Tick each once it is true.
levels.help: Every enhancer works only while it is true. This is the honesty check before anything goes in front of a prospect.

items.label: The scarcity number is true and I would say it to a friend
The deadline is real and I will hold it
I can afford the guarantee if one client in ten claims it
Every bonus can be delivered without extra hours per client, or its cost is in the price

payoff.say: Four tiles, all lit and all true.

levels.checkpoint: All four ticked.

levels.title: Try the guarantee on a real prospect
levels.prompt: Say the guarantee to two real prospects and write down how each one reacted.
levels.help: A guarantee that closes is a keeper. One that worries people is worded wrong, or is the wrong kind for this crowd.

payoff.say: How the guarantee landed.

levels.checkpoint: Two reactions.

levels.title: What it is called today
levels.prompt: Does the offer have a name, and what is it?
levels.help: No name is a fine answer. If there is one, the reveal checks it against the five MAGIC parts.

payoff.say: How much of MAGIC the current name has.

levels.checkpoint: Answered.

levels.title: The offer in one line
levels.prompt: Write the offer as one sentence: who gets what, by when, without what, or else what.
levels.help: A suggestion is built from what the other planets already hold. Edit it until it sounds like you. This line is what the Sky shows when the first ring is cleared.

payoff.say: Your offer in one line.

levels.checkpoint: One sentence you would say out loud.

levels.title: M A G I C
levels.prompt: Fill the five parts. The reveal builds names from them.
levels.help: Magnetic reason why: a season, an event, a milestone, a group. Announce the avatar: who it is for, from the Crowd planet. Give them a goal: the result in a few words. Indicate a time interval: 6 weeks, 30 days. Complete with a container word: Challenge, Blueprint, System, Bootcamp, Program, Accelerator, Masterclass, Intensive.

fields.label: Give them a goal, in a few words

payoff.say: Three names built from the five parts.

levels.checkpoint: All five parts filled.

levels.title: Pick the name
levels.prompt: Choose one of the built names, or write your own version of it.
levels.help: Say it out loud three times. If it is hard to say, it is hard to repeat, and a name lives by being repeated.

payoff.say: The name, on the offer sheet.

levels.checkpoint: A name.

levels.title: Name every piece
levels.prompt: Tick each once it is true of the name and the names of the pieces.
levels.help: The book names the bonuses and the pieces of the stack the same way as the offer: so each sounds like a thing worth having on its own.

items.label: The name says who it is for
The name says the result
The name says how long
It ends in a container word
Each piece of the stack and each bonus has a name that makes sense on its own

payoff.say: The names, checked.

levels.checkpoint: All five ticked.

levels.title: Beat offer fatigue
levels.prompt: Decide now which parts of the wrapper you will refresh, and roughly when.
levels.help: The book's point: an offer gets tired in the market long before the core stops working. Plan to change the name, a bonus, the guarantee, the scarcity or the urgency on a rhythm, and leave the core alone.

payoff.say: The wrapper's refresh plan.

levels.checkpoint: Two or more planned refreshes.

levels.title: Launch
levels.chapter: Section V, your first hundred thousand
levels.prompt: Tick each once it is done.
levels.help: The offer sheet gathers everything the planets hold onto one page. The last two ticks are the launch itself.

items.label: The offer sheet is complete (open it from the Sky)
The price on it is the new price, said without a discount
The guarantee, scarcity and urgency are in the exact words I will use
It went in front of at least ten people who fit the niche
I wrote down every answer

payoff.say: Launched.

levels.checkpoint: All five ticked.

levels.title: First results
levels.prompt: How many people were offered it, how many said yes, and what was collected?
levels.help: The reveal is the close rate at the new price against the old one, and cash per pitch. That is the number the book says to chase: fewer, better clients, paying more.

payoff.say: Close rate, before and after, and cash per pitch.

levels.checkpoint: All three numbers.
